word:greek-nt:G0145.explanation: Sense refers to a capacity for perception or awareness. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, at Hebrews 5:14, and names a sense rather than an action, person, or place. The surrounding verse text is not included, so its specific force there cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is a means of perceiving or recognizing something in ordinary use.

word:greek-nt:G0237.explanation: This word means "elsewhere," "from another way," or "from elsewhere." It points to a different place or direction rather than the one currently being discussed. As an adverb, it describes where something comes from or where it is found, helping distinguish one location or route from another. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, in Mark 1:38 and John 10:1. Its precise force in either verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains movement or location associated with somewhere different.

word:greek-nt:G0394.explanation: This word means “to set before,” describing the act of placing or presenting something in front of someone for consideration. It is an action word: what is set before others is brought into their view or attention. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, once in Acts and once in Galatians. Its exact force in either verse depends on what is being presented and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains bringing something forward before another person.

word:greek-nt:G0404.explanation: This word means “refreshed” or “to refresh”: to bring renewed strength, relief, or encouragement to someone. It describes a restoring effect rather than merely providing information or giving instruction. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in 2 Timothy 1:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains clear: someone’s weariness or burden is eased, and renewed strength or comfort is received.

word:greek-nt:G0552.explanation: Apeiros means inexperienced or unskilled, describing someone not acquainted with a subject.

word:greek-nt:G0615.explanation: Apokteino means to put to death or kill.

word:greek-nt:G0776.explanation: Asitia means lack of food. It can also mean abstinence from food, or fasting.

word:greek-nt:G0817.explanation: Ater means apart from or without.

word:greek-nt:G0963.explanation: Bethany is the name of a place.

word:greek-nt:G1032.explanation: Bryō means to cause something to gush forth or send it forth.

word:greek-nt:G1090.explanation: This verb means “to farm,” describing the work of cultivating land so it can produce a crop. It refers to agricultural labor rather than to the land itself or the harvest. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 6:7. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains the active work of farming and tending cultivated ground.

word:greek-nt:G1124.explanation: Graphe means a writing. It can also mean a passage of Scripture.

word:greek-nt:G1151.explanation: This word refers to a heifer, a young female cow. It is a specific animal term rather than a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Hebrews 9:13. Its precise significance there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself retains this straightforward meaning: a heifer used as an animal in the discussion. The English rendering consistently gives the same meaning.

word:greek-nt:G1393.explanation: Dorkas is the Greek name Dorcas for Tabitha.

word:greek-nt:G1447.explanation: Hebraisti means in Hebrew, or in the Aramaic dialect. It marks the language used for place names and inscriptions.

word:greek-nt:G1520.explanation: Heis means one, referring to a single person or thing.

word:greek-nt:G1582.explanation: This word means “to hang upon,” describing something suspended from or clinging to something else. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 19:48. The basic sense is straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is hanging upon what. Its single occurrence means the word has a focused use in this corpus rather than a broad range of repeated applications.

word:greek-nt:G1601.explanation: Ekpiptō means to fall off or fall away. It describes chains falling off and falling away from grace.

word:greek-nt:G1746«G1744.explanation: This word means to sneak in or to worm one’s way into a place or situation, emphasizing quiet, gradual, or concealed entry. It describes the manner of entering rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Timothy 3:6. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is an unobtrusive entry.

word:greek-nt:G1753.explanation: Energeia means working, action, or productive activity.

word:greek-nt:G1906.explanation: Eperōtēma means an appeal or request. It can also mean a pledge, expressed here as the answer of a good conscience toward God.

word:greek-nt:G2055.explanation: This word means “a goat,” referring to the animal. It is used once in the Greek New Testament, at Matthew 25:33. The plural rendering “goats” reflects how the word appears in that verse, but its basic lexical meaning remains goat. Understanding the word identifies the kind of animal being named; the particular significance it carries in Matthew depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:greek-nt:G2103.explanation: Eubulus is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only once, in 2 Timothy 4:21, and is rendered “Eubulus.” Because this word functions as a person’s name, its basic meaning is identification: it tells the reader who is being mentioned. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the verse’s full wording.

word:greek-nt:G2158.explanation: Euschēmōn means comely, proper, or presentable. It can also describe a person of honorable or prominent standing.

word:greek-nt:G2231.explanation: This word means “reign”: the period during which a ruler governs. It focuses on the ruler’s governing era or dominion rather than naming the ruler himself. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Luke 3:1. Its specific reference there depends on the surrounding historical statement, but the central idea remains the exercise of rule during a defined period. The word therefore describes a ruler’s time of governing and the authority associated with that rule.

word:greek-nt:G2244.explanation: Helikia means age or term of life. It can also mean stature or height.

word:greek-nt:G2312.explanation: This word means “divinely instructed” or “taught by God.” It describes someone whose understanding or conduct has been formed through God’s instruction, emphasizing God as the source of that teaching. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Thessalonians 4:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: receiving instruction that comes from God rather than merely from human teachers.

word:greek-nt:G2389.explanation: Jannes is a personal name referring to an individual named in the Greek New Testament. It does not describe a general quality, action, or object; it identifies a person. The name appears once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:8. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name itself supports only this identification, not further conclusions about the person’s character, actions, or significance. Its English rendering is also “Jannes,” preserving the name rather than translating it into a descriptive meaning.

word:greek-nt:G2442.explanation: Ὁμειρόμενοι means to desire earnestly or love fervently.

word:greek-nt:G2507.explanation: Kathaireō means to take down, pull down, depose, or destroy.

word:greek-nt:G2684.explanation: This word means “to spy” or “to spy on”—to watch someone secretly in order to observe or investigate them. It describes an action rather than a person or object. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Galatians 2:4. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise force there cannot be described further, but the central idea remains secret observation or investigation.

word:greek-nt:G2749.explanation: Keimai means to lie. It can also describe something being set in place. The word can also mean appointed.

word:greek-nt:G2770.explanation: Kerdainō means to gain or acquire. It can describe obtaining more, such as additional talents, or winning a brother back.

word:greek-nt:G2811.explanation: Kleos means glory. Here, it asks what glory there is in patiently enduring being beaten for one's faults.

word:greek-nt:G2864.explanation: Komē means hair, including long hair.

word:greek-nt:G2925.explanation: Krouō means to knock, including at a door to gain admittance. Peter continues knocking until the door is opened.

word:greek-nt:G3027.explanation: Lēstēs means a robber, brigand, or bandit. One account shows robbers stripping and beating a man.

word:greek-nt:G3122.explanation: Malista means most of all or especially, giving particular emphasis to one person or group within a broader statement.

word:greek-nt:G3180.explanation: Methodeia means scheming or craftiness used to deceive.

word:greek-nt:G3346.explanation: Metatrepō means to change or transfer. It can also describe deserting someone.

word:greek-nt:G3405.explanation: This word means “recompense” or “reward”—something given in return for what a person has done or endured. It points to a received return, whether viewed as repayment or as a promised benefit. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Hebrews, where it is consistently rendered “reward.” Its central idea is the outcome granted in response to faithful action, effort, or costly commitment, while the surrounding verse determines the particular situation being discussed.

word:greek-nt:G3540.explanation: This word refers to the mind’s thoughts, understanding, or way of thinking. It describes what a person holds in mind and considers, whether those thoughts are open, affected, directed, or guarded. In the New Testament, it is used six times, chiefly in 2 Corinthians and once in Philippians. Its usual English renderings are “minds” and “thought,” showing that it can refer either to people’s inward understanding or to the thoughts occupying them. The surrounding verse determines its precise emphasis.

word:greek-nt:G3579.explanation: Xenizo means to host or entertain a stranger.

word:greek-nt:G3618.explanation: ᾠκοδόμησεν means to build or erect a building.

word:greek-nt:G3643.explanation: Oligōrei means to despise. It can also mean to make light of something.

word:greek-nt:G3777.explanation: Oute means “and not,” “neither,” or “nor.” It joins paired things or actions under a shared negative, as in “neither death nor life.”

word:greek-nt:G3809.explanation: Paideia means discipline. It includes training and instruction, and can also refer to chastisement.

word:greek-nt:G3830.explanation: Pandocheus means a host or innkeeper.

word:greek-nt:G3892.explanation: Paranomia means transgression, a violation of law. It can also describe lawlessness or wrongdoing, expressed as iniquity or disobedience.

word:greek-nt:G4079.explanation: Pedalion means the rudder of a ship.

word:greek-nt:G4105.explanation: Planao means to lead astray or deceive.

word:greek-nt:G4277.explanation: This Greek New Testament verb means “to foretell” or “to predict”—to state beforehand what will happen. It refers to announcing something in advance rather than merely describing an event after it occurs. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, in Galatians 5:21 and 1 Thessalonians 4:6. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic idea remains speaking beforehand about a future matter.

word:greek-nt:G4295.explanation: This word means “to be set before” or “to set before,” describing something placed in front of someone or presented for attention. It can express an object, purpose, goal, or situation that is put before people as something to consider or pursue. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including passages in 2 Corinthians, Hebrews, and Jude. Its precise force in any one verse depends on what is being placed before the reader or hearer.

word:greek-nt:G4318.explanation: This word means “access”—the ability to approach or enter into someone’s presence. In the New Testament, it describes the believer’s welcome into God’s presence and the resulting confidence to draw near. It occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, appearing once in Romans and twice in Ephesians. Its repeated use in these letters connects access with the standing believers have through Christ, though the precise emphasis in each verse comes from its surrounding context.

word:greek-nt:G4422.explanation: This word describes being startled or frightened. It can express the sudden alarm a person feels or the action of causing someone to become afraid. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, both in Luke, so its meaning is clear but its use is limited. The surrounding passage determines whether the word emphasizes the person who is frightened or the effect that produces fear. Its two recorded uses appear in Luke 21:9 and Luke 24:37.

word:greek-nt:G4480.explanation: Rhede means a chariot or carriage.

word:greek-nt:G4714.explanation: Stasis means insurrection. It can also mean dissension.

word:greek-nt:G4761.explanation: Strebloō means to twist or distort language. It describes twisting things that are hard to understand and the other Scriptures.

word:greek-nt:G4813.explanation: This word means “to rob”: to take something from another person unlawfully. It describes the act of seizing what does not belong to you, rather than simply receiving or borrowing it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 11:8. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular situation in which Paul used it, but the word itself points plainly to wrongful taking or plundering.

word:greek-nt:G4848.explanation: This word means “to go with,” describing people traveling or moving along together. It presents going with others as a shared movement rather than simply being present in the same place. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in the Gospels, and its meaning remains centered on accompanying others. The surrounding verse determines who is going together and why, but the word itself emphasizes joining someone’s journey or proceeding alongside them.

word:greek-nt:G4934.explanation: Syntithemi means to agree or make an agreement with others.

word:greek-nt:G4941.explanation: Syntyche is a personal name, referring to a woman named Syntyche. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Philippians 4:2, and the English translations retain it as “Syntyche.” The surrounding verse is needed to explain her specific role in that passage; the name itself identifies the person.

word:greek-nt:G5072.explanation: Tetramēnos means a period of four months.

word:greek-nt:G5191.explanation: Hyakinthinos means dark purple or blue, like hyacinth. It describes blue breastplates in the vision.

word:greek-nt:G5238.explanation: This word means “beyond,” expressing something that lies farther than a stated point, limit, or boundary. It directs attention past what has already been reached or considered. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 10:16. Its basic sense is spatial or figurative extension beyond a recognized limit, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being exceeded. The word itself emphasizes moving or reaching farther than the present boundary.

word:greek-nt:G5317.explanation: Peleg is a personal name identifying a person, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, rendered “Peleg,” at Luke 3:35. Because the available material provides the name but not the surrounding verse text, its significance in that particular passage cannot be described further here. Its ordinary lexical role is simply to identify Peleg as an individual named in the New Testament record.

word:greek-nt:G5421.explanation: Phrear means a pit. It can also mean a well or refer to an abyss.

word:greek-nt:G5454.explanation: Phōleos means a hole or den, such as the holes of foxes.

word:greek-nt:G5533.explanation: This word means “debtor”: a person who owes money or some other obligation to another. It describes people viewed in relation to what they are required to repay, rather than focusing on the lender or the debt itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the central idea remains someone who is obligated because something is owed.

word:greek-nt:G5568.explanation: Psalmos means a psalm or song of praise. It can also refer to the book of Psalms.

word:greek-nt:G5586.explanation: Psēphos means a small stone or pebble. It can also mean a vote.

word:greek-nt:G5616.explanation: Hōsei means like, as if, or as it were. With numbers, it means about.
